opening: John Glasgow, born 10 April 1767, is the strongest identity match for the John Glasco who headed Inishrush house 2 in 1831. Family Bibles, his 1847 letter and the Drimbolg church network support that identification. They do not prove that Adam Glasgow was his brother or identify John's parents; Alexander Glasgow-951 should not be attached as his child.

position.answer: The Inishrush identity is strongly supported, while John's parents and exact relationship to Adam remain unresolved.
points: The family Bible records John's birth, marriage and nine children but names no parents and contains no Alexander.
The 1831 Inishrush household closely fits the surviving Bible family after married or deceased children are accounted for.
A second family Bible and John's 1847 letter independently connect this family to Inishrush and the Drimbolg Reformed Presbyterian network.
The 1830 Ohio census household is not this John: its head was aged 40–49, while John was 63.

evidence_questions.title: Why is John identified with the 1831 Inishrush householder?
evidence_questions.answer: The Bible family, place evidence, church network and near-exact household reconstruction make this the strongest identity match.
evidence_questions.reasoning: The family register establishes John's nuclear family; the McKeown Bible and John's own letter independently place that family at Inishrush. The surviving household members closely reproduce the 1831 totals.
evidence_questions.limitation: The 1831 return names only the head, and published transcriptions disagree about denomination.
evidence_questions.missing: The original 1831 return and Drimbolg session material capable of naming household relationships.

evidence_questions.title: Do the records identify John's parents or a brother Adam?
evidence_questions.answer: No. Adam cannot be John's father on age grounds; brother and cousin remain possible, but neither is proved.
evidence_questions.reasoning: The two men headed separate Inishrush households and shared a local religious and social network. Naming patterns suggest an older Adam and Maria, but no record supplies a kin term or shared parent.
evidence_questions.limitation: Naming custom and proximity are clues, not relationship evidence.
evidence_questions.missing: A church, estate, deed, probate or family record that directly names a parent or sibling.

evidence_questions.title: Did the identified church periodical publish John's obituary?
evidence_questions.answer: No John Glasgow obituary was found in the original 1851–52 volume.
evidence_questions.reasoning: The full-view volume, its search results and the final obituary pages following John's 23 December 1851 death were inspected.
evidence_questions.limitation: This is a bounded negative for volume 15; it cannot exclude a brief unindexed notice elsewhere in the periodical.
evidence_questions.missing: Guernsey County probate-case indexes and the congregation's underlying admissions or session records.

bible-john-mary.recorded_statement: John was born 10 April 1767, married Mary on 21 May 1798 and had nine recorded children.
bible-john-mary.relevance: Defines the family used to test the 1831 household.
bible-john-mary.limitation: Later hands entered some events; no parent or marriage place is given.

census-inishrush-1831.recorded_statement: John Glasco headed Inishrush house 2 with four males and four females.
census-inishrush-1831.relevance: The count closely matches John's surviving household family.

bible-mckeown.recorded_statement: John's grandson was born at Inishrush in 1821 and baptised by Rev. Joseph Orr.
bible-mckeown.relevance: Provides independent descendant evidence for place and congregation.
bible-mckeown.limitation: It does not name John's parents.

letter-john-1847.recorded_statement: John recalled family life at Inishrush and relayed detailed news from its local network.
letter-john-1847.relevance: Directly associates the emigrant John with Inishrush.
letter-john-1847.limitation: The reported local James remains an identity inference.

bible-john-mary.recorded_statement: The register begins with John and Mary and their children.
bible-john-mary.relevance: Its child order supports a naming-pattern hypothesis.

census-inishrush-1831.recorded_statement: John and Adam headed separate households in the same townland.
census-inishrush-1831.relevance: Supports association and excludes a single household.

periodical-rp-1852.recorded_statement: The final obituary group names Catherine Kennedy, Elizabeth Carson, Hannah Walker and Ebenezer Craig, not John Glasgow.
periodical-rp-1852.relevance: Closes the specifically identified denominational volume as a formal-obituary source.
periodical-rp-1852.limitation: A short unindexed notice elsewhere is not excluded.

research_tasks.what: Inspect the Drimbolg congregation's underlying admissions and session records for John and Adam Glasgow.
research_tasks.tests: Tests identity, migration and an explicit relationship between the two Inishrush households.
research_tasks.matters: A kin term, transfer, residence or family admission would outweigh naming-pattern inference.

research_tasks.what: Check the Guernsey County probate case-file index for an intestate administration after John's 1851 death.
research_tasks.tests: Tests for heirs, relatives and an estate file despite the absence of a recorded will.
research_tasks.matters: The public will indexes contain no Glasgow testator, but do not exclude administration.

research_tasks.what: Recover Hiltner source S17, Descendants of John Glasgow.pdf / Glasgow Register Report.doc.
research_tasks.tests: Tests whether the cited 2018 compilation preserves sourced parentage or migration evidence.
research_tasks.matters: Its title is not evidence until the underlying files and citations are recovered.
